summary: Describes the Transaction Key (TKEY) resource record, which can establish shared secret keys between a DNS resolver and server in several modes. Those keys can then secure later DNS messages.

eli5.summary: A DNS client and server need a shared secret code word. This describes ways to agree on one safely.

questions: how to establish a shared secret with dns
what is the tkey record type number
subtitle: How a DNS resolver and server agree on a shared secret key, so later messages can be authenticated with TSIG.

tldr.problem: TSIG authenticates DNS messages with shared secret keys, but it offers no way to set those keys up other than exchanging them by hand.
tldr.mechanism: The TKEY resource record (type 249) carries a mode, a validity period and key data in an ordinary DNS query and response. Modes cover Diffie-Hellman, GSS-API, server assigned keys, resolver assigned keys and key deletion.
tldr.outcome: A resolver and server can create and delete shared secrets in-band. The RFC states that it gives no protection against denial of service, and it is updated by RFC 6895.

today: RFC 2930 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6895. It has not been obsoleted. It builds on TSIG, defined in RFC 2845.

sections.title: Why DNS Needs Key Setup
sections.content:
RFC 2845 defines TSIG, which authenticates DNS queries and responses with shared secret keys. It provides no way to set up such keys except manual exchange. RFC 2930 adds the TKEY resource record, usable in several modes, to establish and delete shared secrets between a DNS resolver and a server.

TKEY keys are tied to servers and resolvers, not to zones. They can authenticate queries and responses, but they do not provide zone-based data origin or denial authentication. Here, the term resolver also covers the part of a server that makes zone transfer queries and forwards recursive queries.

Some modes perform encryption, which the RFC notes may affect export or import status in some countries. The affected modes are server assigned and resolver assigned.
sections.eli5: DNS has a way to sign messages with a shared secret, but no safe way to pick that secret. TKEY fills that gap.

sections.title: The TKEY Record
sections.content:
TKEY is a resource record with RR type code 249. Its data holds an Algorithm name, Inception and Expiration times, a Mode, an Error code, a Key Size and Key Data, and an Other Size and Other Data pair that this specification does not use.

The record's class SHOULD be 255 (ANY) and its TTL SHOULD be zero, so that older DNS implementations do not cache it. TKEY is a meta-RR: it is not stored or cached in DNS and does not appear in zone files. There MUST NOT be more than one TKEY RR in a query or response.

The Name field names the key. A server only holds one set of keying material for a given name, and trying to set another returns BADNAME. For a key created from a query with the root as owner name, the server SHOULD build a globally unique name from a pseudo-random label and the server's own domain name. Inception and expiration are seconds since 1 January 1970, so both sides need the same idea of the time, and any time synchronization used MUST be done securely.
sections.eli5: The record is a form with boxes for the name of the secret, which method you are using, how long it lasts, and the secret data itself.

sections.title: Modes and Error Codes
sections.content:
The Mode field says how the key is agreed or what the message is for. Servers and resolvers MUST implement the Diffie-Hellman mode and the key deletion mode. All other modes are OPTIONAL. A server that gets a mode it does not support returns BADMODE.

The Error field is an extended RCODE. The new values are 19 (BADMODE), 20 (BADNAME) and 21 (BADALG). When the TKEY error is non-zero in a response to a TKEY query, the DNS header RCODE still indicates no error.

A server unwilling to keep the state a key requires MUST return an error such as NOTIMP or REFUSED. Resolvers are free to ignore TKEY records they receive.
sections.eli5: There are five ways to agree on a secret, like five different handshakes. Every computer has to know at least the Diffie-Hellman handshake and how to cancel a secret.

sections.title: Key Agreement by Query
sections.content:
Keys are set up with DNS requests of query type TKEY, with a TKEY RR in the additional section. These queries SHOULD NOT be flagged recursive.

In Diffie-Hellman mode, the resolver sends its DH KEY RR and a nonce in the TKEY key data. The server answers with its own DH KEY RR and another nonce. Both sides compute the same DH value and mix in the nonces: the keying material is the DH value XORed with the MD5 digests of each nonce suffixed by the DH value, concatenated.

In GSS-API mode, the two sides exchange GSS-API tokens in the key data, described in a separate document. Inception and expiry are ignored there.

In server assigned mode, the server generates the key and returns it encrypted under the resolver's public key in the KEY RR sent with the query. In resolver assigned mode, the resolver encrypts the key under a server public key and sends it. The resolver KEY RR in a server assigned query MUST be authenticated, and resolver assigned queries MUST be authenticated with a TSIG or SIG(0), or an attacker could choose or learn the key.

For key deletion, a server MUST implement deletion on an authenticated request naming the key, and returns BADNAME if it does not know the key. A server may also include a deletion TKEY spontaneously in the additional section of a response, which SHOULD be authenticated.
sections.eli5: In the main method, both sides each add a secret ingredient and stir them together, so they end up with the same dish without ever telling anyone the recipe.

sections.title: Authentication and Limits
sections.content:
Except in GSS-API mode, TKEY responses MUST be authenticated, using a previously established TSIG secret or a SIG(0) public key, and never with a key the same message is providing. TKEY queries MUST also be authenticated for all modes except GSS-API and, under some circumstances, server assignment mode. If no required authentication is present, NOTAUTH MUST be returned.

To stop replay after about 136 years (232 seconds), the key used to authenticate a TKEY message MUST NOT have a lifetime of more than about 68 years (231 minus 1 seconds).

For encrypted modes the keying material is encrypted directly under the public key in the KEY RR; with RSA, RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 from PKCS#1 is used. The RFC's own security section says the whole specification is about secure establishment of a shared secret for TSIG, and that protection against denial of service is not provided.
sections.eli5: The secret handshake itself has to be checked with something you already trust, never with something the stranger hands you. The RFC says it cannot stop someone from simply flooding the server.

items.label: Server assignment
items.desc: Server generates the key and encrypts it for the resolver.

items.label: Diffie-Hellman exchange
items.desc: Both sides derive the key; MUST be implemented.

items.label: GSS-API negotiation
items.desc: GSS-API tokens carried in the key data.

items.label: Resolver assignment
items.desc: Resolver generates the key and encrypts it for the server.

items.label: Key deletion
items.desc: Discards a key; MUST be implemented.

messages.note: Additional section: TKEY (DH mode, nonce) and resolver DH KEY RR.

messages.label: Response with TKEY
messages.note: Answer section: TKEY with server nonce and server DH KEY RR; resolver KEY echoed.
